claim: Postnatal long bones of mice contain at least two types of bone progenitors with bona fide skeletal stem cell (SSC) characteristics.
source: Here we show, through comprehensive functional and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, that postnatal long bones of mice contain at least two types of bone progenitors with bona fide skeletal stem cell (SSC) characteristics.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assays and single-cell RNA sequencing data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: An early osteochondral SSC (ocSSC) facilitates long bone growth and repair.
source: An early osteochondral SSC (ocSSC) facilitates long bone growth and repair, while a second type, a perivascular SSC (pvSSC), co-emerges with long bone marrow and contributes to shape the hematopoietic stem cell niche and regenerative demand.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data showing ocSSC accumulation during fracture regeneration and their presence in early limb development.

claim: A perivascular SSC (pvSSC) co-emerges with long bone marrow and contributes to shape the hematopoietic stem cell niche and regenerative demand.
source: An early osteochondral SSC (ocSSC) facilitates long bone growth and repair, while a second type, a perivascular SSC (pvSSC), co-emerges with long bone marrow and contributes to shape the hematopoietic stem cell niche and regenerative demand.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing pvSSC emergence timing coinciding with HSC detection and their increase after irradiation.

claim: pvSSCs, but not ocSSCs, are the origin of bone marrow adipose tissue.
source: We establish that pvSSCs, but not ocSSCs, are the origin of bone marrow adipose tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro and in vivo differentiation assays showing adipogenic potential only in pvSSCs.

claim: Bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) with stem cell-like characteristics are mainly enriched either by plastic adherence or single fluorescence labeling in reporter mouse lines.
source: To date, bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) with stem cell-like characteristics are mainly enriched either by plastic adherence or single fluorescence labeling in reporter mouse lines (Kfoury and Scadden, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BMSCs have been improperly considered stem cells if they undergo osteogenic, chondrogenic, and adipogenic differentiation in vitro and express a specific set of surface markers when expanded in cultures while omitting tests for single-cell self-renewal and multipotency.
source: BMSCs have been improperly considered stem cells if they undergo osteogenic, chondrogenic, and adipogenic differentiation in vitro and express a specific set of surface markers when expanded in cultures while omitting tests for single-cell self-renewal and multipotency (Dominici et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work and represents a critique of existing methodology.

claim: Leptin receptor (LepR)-labeled cells mark SSCs but also label more mature cell types such as endothelial cells, pre-osteoblasts, osteoblasts, and chondrocytes of long bones.
source: Leptin receptor (LepR)-labeled cells, for example, have long been called SSCs, but they also label more mature cell types such as endothelial cells, pre-osteoblasts, osteoblasts, and chondrocytes of long bones (Zhou et al., 2014; Tikhonova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Osteochondrogenic SSCs (ocSSCs) are restricted to bone, cartilage, and stromal lineage output but do not give rise to bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT).
source: These osteochondrogenic SSCs (ocSSCs) are restricted to bone, cartilage, and stromal lineage output but do not give rise to bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) (Ambrosi and Schulz, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work and data in the manuscript.

claim: A perivascular SSC (pvSSC) with tri-lineage potential has been shown to be the main source of bone marrow adipocytes.
source: Strikingly, using a different set of surface markers, a perivascular SSC (pvSSC) with tri-lineage potential has been shown to be the main source of bone marrow adipocytes, implying the existence of multiple stem cell-like populations (Ambrosi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A recent scRNAseq analysis on bone marrow mesenchyme inferred that at least two origins for osteogenic cell fates in the bone marrow exist.
source: In support of this possibility, a recent scRNAseq analysis on bone marrow mesenchyme also inferred that at least two origins for osteogenic cell fates in the bone marrow exist (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ocSSCs and pvSSCs display high clonogenic activity in renal capsule transplants.
source: We observed high clonal activity in transplants with ocSSCs and pvSSCs, which is a hallmark of stem cell activity (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 1C using Rainbow mice.

claim: ocSSC and pvSSC grafts form ossicles with bone and cartilage capable of generating an ectopic hematopoietic niche through recruitment of host-derived blood and immune cells.
source: 4-week grafts of both cell populations formed ossicles with bone and cartilage capable of generating an ectopic hematopoietic niche through recruitment of host-derived blood and immune cells (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and flow cytometry data from renal capsule transplants.

claim: Only pvSSC-derived grafts contained adipocytes.
source: As expected, only pvSSC-derived grafts contained adipocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis of renal capsule transplants shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Phenotypic ocSSCs and pvSSCs remained present in 4-week grafts after dissociation.
source: To confirm the long-term self-renewal of SSCs, we dissociated 4-week grafts for FACS analysis and found, in line with in vitro expanded cells, that phenotypic ocSSCs and pvSSCs remained present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data demonstrating self-renewal capacity.

claim: Freshly bulk-isolated ocSSCs and pvSSCs showed high clonogenic and osteochondrogenic differentiation potential in vitro.
source: Fibroblast colony-forming unit (CFU-F) and tri-lineage differentiation assays on freshly bulk-isolated ocSSCs and pvSSCs also showed high clonogenic and osteochondrogenic differentiation potential in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU-F and differentiation assay data.

claim: ocSSCs did not acquire adipogenic potential even under strong adipogenic stimuli and when isolated from BMAT-rich long bones of 2-year-old mice.
source: Strikingly, in comparison to pvSSCs, ocSSCs did not acquire adipogenic potential even under strong adipogenic stimuli and when isolated from BMAT-rich long bones of 2-year-old mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by adipogenic differentiation assay data from aged mice.

claim: Single-clone CFUs derived from individual sorted ocSSCs and pvSSCs showed differences in lineage potential.
source: This difference in lineage potential was also observed in single-clone CFUs derived from individual sorted ocSSCs and pvSSCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell clonal differentiation assay data.

claim: Osteochondrogenic lineage output was observed in both ocSSC and pvSSC intratibial transplants, and only pvSSCs generated perilipin-positive bone marrow adipocytes.
source: Again, osteochondrogenic lineage output was observed in both cell types, and only pvSSCs generated perilipin-positive bone marrow adipocytes (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistological staining data from intratibial transplants.

claim: ocSSCs/BCSPs are enriched in micro-dissected non-marrow fractions of femurs.
source: In agreement with the original reports, we found that ocSSCs/BCSPs are enriched in micro-dissected non-marrow fractions of femurs while pvSSCs and the committed APCs are more evenly distributed but accumulate at the ends of long bones where coincidentally BMAT first appears (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Chan et al., 2015; Scheller et al., 2015; Ambrosi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis of micro-dissected bone regions and citations to previous work.

claim: pvSSCs and committed APCs are more evenly distributed but accumulate at the ends of long bones where BMAT first appears.
source: In agreement with the original reports, we found that ocSSCs/BCSPs are enriched in micro-dissected non-marrow fractions of femurs while pvSSCs and the committed APCs are more evenly distributed but accumulate at the ends of long bones where coincidentally BMAT first appears (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Chan et al., 2015; Scheller et al., 2015; Ambrosi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis of micro-dissected bone regions and citations to previous work.

claim: Both ocSSC and pvSSC types were found on the periosteum.
source: Of note, both SSC types were found on the periosteum, a site described to harbor a distinct stem cell for bone regeneration (Debnath et al., 2018; Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data and citations to previous work.

claim: ocSSCs are present in high abundance at the early stages of limb development (E13.5).
source: Flow cytometric analysis of long bones at different timepoints during skeletal maturation further revealed that ocSSCs are present in high abundance at the early stages of limb development (E13.5), linking them to bone formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data across developmental timepoints.

claim: pvSSCs are first detectable around E15.5, similar to hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) detection in mouse bone marrow, and peak perinatally.
source: Contrastingly, pvSSCs are first detectable around E15.5, similar to hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) detection in mouse bone marrow, and peak perinatally (Figure 2B; Rowe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data across developmental timepoints and a citation to previous work on HSC detection.

claim: Transplanted ≤E13.5 tibias failed to develop GFP-labeled diaphyseal bone marrow adipocytes whereas ≥P1 tibia bones strongly accumulated adipocytes below the growth plate.
source: Interestingly, transplanted ≤E13.5 tibias failed to develop GFP-labeled diaphyseal bone marrow adipocytes whereas ≥P1 tibia bones strongly accumulated adipocytes below the growth plate in this experimental setting (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by renal capsule transplant data of whole bones from different developmental stages.

claim: Sca1 expression was virtually absent in newborn and 8-week-old uninjured long bone as well as post-fracture day-5 and -15 ocSSCs/BCSPs.
source: We found that Sca1 expression was virtually absent in newborn and 8-week-old uninjured long bone as well as post-fracture day-5 and -15 ocSSCs/BCSPs (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data showing Sca1 expression patterns.

claim: The majority of Sca1-positive cells in the ocSSC lineage tree were contained in the Tie2-positive fraction.
source: Analysis of the ocSSC lineage tree revealed that the majority of Sca1-positive cells were contained in the Tie2-positive fraction, in agreement with our earlier work showing adipogenic potential of that population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F; Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data and a citation to previous work.

claim: ocSSCs from E13.5 and newborn mice did not give rise to pvSSCs/APCs in 4-week renal grafts, and pvSSC-derived grafts did not generate ocSSCs/BCSPs.
source: Importantly, ocSSCs from E13.5 and newborn mice did not give rise to pvSSCs/APCs in 4-week renal grafts, and pvSSC-derived grafts did not generate ocSSCs/BCSPs (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis of renal graft-derived cells.

claim: ocSSC and pvSSC clustered separately in single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.
source: Strikingly, ocSSC and pvSSC clustered separately with Ly6a/Sca1 expression pattern, confirming cell-type specificity (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq clustering analysis.

claim: Gene ontology analysis demonstrated a strong association of ocSSCs with skeletal development and formation, while pvSSC genes were linked to extracellular matrix organization and regulation of hematopoietic cell types.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed genes between both cell types through GO Biological Processes demonstrated a strong association of ocSSCs with skeletal development and formation, while pvSSC genes were linked to extracellular matrix organization and regulation of hematopoietic cell types (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: The ocSSC population expressed much higher levels of commonly known osteochondrogenic genes (Acan, Col2a1, Pthr1, Spp1).
source: The ocSSC population also expressed much higher levels of commonly known osteochondrogenic genes (Acan, Col2a1, Pthr1, Spp1), whereas pvSSCs exhibited elevated gene counts for fibroblast markers (Pdgfra, Postn, Dpt) and factors related to hematopoietic interactions (Cxcl12, Igf1, Rarres2) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data.

claim: pvSSCs exhibited elevated gene counts for fibroblast markers (Pdgfra, Postn, Dpt) and factors related to hematopoietic interactions (Cxcl12, Igf1, Rarres2).
source: The ocSSC population also expressed much higher levels of commonly known osteochondrogenic genes (Acan, Col2a1, Pthr1, Spp1), whereas pvSSCs exhibited elevated gene counts for fibroblast markers (Pdgfra, Postn, Dpt) and factors related to hematopoietic interactions (Cxcl12, Igf1, Rarres2) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data.

claim: pvSSCs and their downstream APCs were strongly increased compared to non-irradiated mice 2 weeks after sublethal irradiation.
source: pvSSCs and their downstream APCs were strongly increased compared to non-irradiated mice in line with their potential role in supporting hematopoietic recovery and the increase in BMAT seen upon radiation (Naveiras et al., 2009), while irradiation-sensitive ocSSC/BCSPs showed a decline in numbers (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data after irradiation and a citation to previous work.

claim: Irradiation-sensitive ocSSC/BCSPs showed a decline in numbers after sublethal irradiation.
source: pvSSCs and their downstream APCs were strongly increased compared to non-irradiated mice in line with their potential role in supporting hematopoietic recovery and the increase in BMAT seen upon radiation (Naveiras et al., 2009), while irradiation-sensitive ocSSC/BCSPs showed a decline in numbers (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data after irradiation.

claim: ocSSCs accumulate significantly more in callus tissue compared to pvSSCs during bi-cortical fracture regeneration.
source: In contrast, when we assessed the prevalence of SSC types during bi-cortical fracture regeneration, we found ocSSCs to accumulate significantly more in callus tissue compared to pvSSCs as expected from their pivotal role in skeletal repair (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F; Marecic et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data during fracture healing and a citation to previous work.

claim: Bone anabolic ocSSCs were significantly reduced with age in 30-month-old mice compared to 2-month-old mice.
source: While bone anabolic ocSSCs were significantly reduced with age, bone marrow adipocytes forming pvSSCs/APCs were increased (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data comparing young and aged mice.

claim: Bone marrow adipocyte-forming pvSSCs/APCs were increased with age in 30-month-old mice compared to 2-month-old mice.
source: While bone anabolic ocSSCs were significantly reduced with age, bone marrow adipocytes forming pvSSCs/APCs were increased (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data comparing young and aged mice.

claim: In co-transplantation experiments, ocSSCs were a key contributor to osteochondrogenic tissue and reticular cells, whereas pvSSC-derived cells were more prevalent in areas anatomically close to host-derived hematopoietic tissue.
source: Finally, co-transplantation of equal numbers of purified, uniquely labeled SSC types under the renal capsule of NSG mice generated ossicles with ocSSCs as a key contributor to osteochondrogenic tissue and reticular cells, whereas pvSSC-derived cells were more prevalent in areas anatomically close to host-derived hematopoietic tissue (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis of co-transplantation experiments.

claim: Genes reported to describe SSC populations, for example, Pthrp, Ctsk, Cxcl12, and Osx, show variable expression within and between ocSSCs and pvSSCs.
source: scRNAseq data suggested that genes reported to describe SSC populations, for example, Pthrp, Ctsk, Cxcl12, and Osx, show variable expression within and between ocSSCs and pvSSCs (Figure 4B; Greenbaum et al., 2013; Mizoguchi et al., 2014; Mizuhashi et al., 2018; Debnath et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data and citations to previous work.

claim: Reporter strains for labeling chondrocytes (Col2a1, Acan) and osteoblasts (Col1a1, Spp1) show expression in stem cell-like populations.
source: Similarly, reporter strains for labeling more mature cell types such as chondrocytes (Col2a1, Acan) and osteoblasts (Col1a1, Spp1) also show expression in stem cell-like populations (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data.

claim: LepR expression was found in both ocSSC and pvSSC cell types.
source: When we analyzed LepR expression on ocSSC/pvSSC lineage populations by FACS, we found LepR expression in both cell types (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data.

claim: Separating ocSSCs or pvSSCs into LepR-positive and -negative fractions did not alter CFU-F capacity.
source: Separating ocSSCs or pvSSCs into LepR-positive and -negative fractions did not alter CFU-F capacity (Figure 4D) and potential to give rise to osteocalcin-expressing osteoblasts in vitro (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU-F assay data.

claim: Separating ocSSCs or pvSSCs into LepR-positive and -negative fractions did not alter potential to give rise to osteocalcin-expressing osteoblasts in vitro.
source: Separating ocSSCs or pvSSCs into LepR-positive and -negative fractions did not alter CFU-F capacity (Figure 4D) and potential to give rise to osteocalcin-expressing osteoblasts in vitro (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by osteogenic differentiation assay data.

claim: Leiden clustering yielded three subclusters for ocSSCs while pvSSCs were homogeneous in their overall gene signature.
source: To assess the diversity within ocSSC and pvSSC variants, we conducted Leiden clustering on our scRNAseq dataset. This yielded three subclusters for ocSSCs while pvSSCs were homogeneous in their overall gene signature (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Leiden clustering analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 were enriched for marker genes of chondrogenic and osteogenic fates, respectively.
source: Looking at the top differentially expressed genes between the four clusters, we found that clusters 3 and 4 were enriched for marker genes of chondrogenic and osteogenic fates, respectively (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Cluster 1 (pvSSCs) and cluster 2 were enriched for stem cell-associated genes.
source: Further, cluster 1 (pvSSCs) and cluster 2 were enriched for stem cell-associated genes (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 showed pathway enrichment related to active bone formation processes.
source: whereas clusters 3 and 4 showed pathway enrichment related to active bone formation processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Cell cycle status and CytoTrace analysis inferred that osteochondrogenic SSC-enriched clusters were more active.
source: Cell cycle status and CytoTrace analysis additionally inferred that osteochondrogenic SSC-enriched clusters were more active (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle and CytoTrace analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Leiden clusters revealed patterns in expression of combinations of ligands and cognate receptors that are highly suggestive of crosstalk between ocSSCs and pvSSCs.
source: Leiden clusters revealed patterns in expression of combinations of ligands and cognate receptors that are highly suggestive of crosstalk between ocSSCs and pvSSCs (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ligand-receptor expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Cells of cluster 1 (pvSSCs) expressed Tgfb2/Tgfb3 and Wnt ligand genes, which might support the specific fate commitment of ocSSCs enriched in clusters 2–4 that expressed respective receptors.
source: For example, cells of cluster 1 (pvSSCs) expressed Tgfb2/Tgfb3 and Wnt ligand genes, well-known pro-chondrogenic and -osteogenic signals, which might support the specific fate commitment of ocSSCs enriched in clusters 2–4 that expressed respective receptors (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ligand-receptor expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Bmp, Tgfa, and Egf ligands from cells of primed clusters 3 and 4 might signal back to pvSSCs, which express the canonical cognate receptor genes to these pathways.
source: Reversely, Bmp, Tgfa, and Egf ligands from cells of primed clusters 3 and 4 might also signal back to pvSSCs, which express the canonical cognate receptor genes to these pathways, implying feedback regulation across SSC types (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ligand-receptor expression analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Cadherin-13 (Cdh13) is a new marker gene for the most stem cell-like cluster 1 (pvSSC).
source: Taking advantage of our scRNAseq dataset, we identified cadherin-13 (Cdh13), the receptor for the adipogenic factor adiponectin (Hug et al., 2004), and Wnt inhibitory factor-1 (Wif1), previously identified to be expressed in a small subset of BMSCs (Tikhonova et al., 2019), as new marker genes for the most stem cell-like clusters 1 (pvSSC) and 2 (ocSSC), respectively (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data and citations to previous work.

claim: Wnt inhibitory factor-1 (Wif1) is a new marker gene for the most stem cell-like cluster 2 (ocSSC).
source: Taking advantage of our scRNAseq dataset, we identified cadherin-13 (Cdh13), the receptor for the adipogenic factor adiponectin (Hug et al., 2004), and Wnt inhibitory factor-1 (Wif1), previously identified to be expressed in a small subset of BMSCs (Tikhonova et al., 2019), as new marker genes for the most stem cell-like clusters 1 (pvSSC) and 2 (ocSSC), respectively (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq gene expression data and citations to previous work.

claim: In situ hybridization confirmed a restricted expression of Wif1 in the resting and proliferative zones of the growth plate.
source: In situ hybridization by RNAscope confirmed a restricted expression of Wif1 in the resting and proliferative zones of the growth plate, while Cdh13 was absent and found in cells located in the bone marrow close to endomucin-expressing vasculature (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data.

claim: Cdh13 was absent in the growth plate and found in cells located in the bone marrow close to endomucin-expressing vasculature.
source: In situ hybridization by RNAscope confirmed a restricted expression of Wif1 in the resting and proliferative zones of the growth plate, while Cdh13 was absent and found in cells located in the bone marrow close to endomucin-expressing vasculature (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data.

claim: Wif1- and Cdh13-expressing cells were found among periosteal cells.
source: As observed via flow cytometric analysis, Wif1- and Cdh13-expressing cells were also found among periosteal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data.

claim: The osteochondral SSC is closely associated with marrow-free spaces such as the growth plate or periosteum.
source: The osteochondral SSC, closely associated with marrow-free spaces such as the growth plate or periosteum, was highly prevalent in early limb development, remained present in low numbers throughout adulthood, and could be activated to accumulate upon injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical localization data and developmental timepoint analysis.

claim: ocSSCs never gave rise to BMAT and may be the main source of osteochondrogenic tissue in long bones.
source: We also showed that ocSSCs never gave rise to BMAT and may be the main source of osteochondrogenic tissue in long bones.
evidence: The claim is supported by differentiation assay data and transplantation experiments.

claim: ocSSCs might be the SSC type exclusively targeted by the Osx-Cre reporter line that has been previously described to label cells that form bone and transient stromal cells in the fetal skeleton, while being restricted to osteolineages during adulthood.
source: Therefore, ocSSCs might be the SSC type exclusively targeted by the Osx-Cre reporter line that has been previously described to label cells that form bone and transient stromal cells in the fetal skeleton, while being restricted to osteolineages during adulthood (Mizoguchi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and a citation to previous work.

claim: ocSSCs are included as subpopulations of Pthrp-expressing growth plate and Ctsk-expressing periosteal stem and progenitor cell types.
source: Based on recent reports, ocSSCs are included as subpopulations of Pthrp-expressing growth plate and Ctsk-expressing periosteal stem and progenitor cell types (Debnath et al., 2018; Mizuhashi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and gene expression data.

claim: pvSSCs occurred at a later embryonic stage in sync with the homing of HSCs to bone marrow niches.
source: pvSSCs, demonstrated to be essential for BMAT development, occurred at a later embryonic stage in sync with the homing of HSCs to bone marrow niches (Figure 2B–C; Rowe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timepoint analysis and a citation to previous work.

claim: A critical role for mesenchymal cell types to maintain HSC quiescence has long been established.
source: A critical role for mesenchymal cell types to maintain HSC quiescence has long been established (Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When intratibially injected, pvSSCs seemed to distribute more evenly throughout the marrow, potentially to HSC niches, whereas ocSSC-derived cells mainly aggregated in a more confined space.
source: When intratibially injected, pvSSCs also seemed to distribute more evenly throughout the marrow, potentially to HSC niches, whereas ocSSC-derived cells mainly aggregated in a more confined space (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis of intratibial transplants.

claim: Recent scRNAseq studies have found abundant adipo-primed cell populations in the bone marrow that were implied to be a major reservoir of pro-hematopoietic, pro-vascular, and anti-osteogenic factors.
source: In line with our scRNAseq expression data on pvSSCs, recent scRNAseq studies have found abundant adipo-primed cell populations in the bone marrow that were implied to be a major reservoir of pro-hematopoietic, pro-vascular, and anti-osteogenic factors (Zhong et al., 2020; Tikhonova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: pvSSCs and their downstream APCs were increased in frequency in older mice.
source: Finally, in contrast to ocSSCs, pvSSCs and their downstream APCs were increased in frequency in older mice (Figure 3G) and thus correlate with the observation of higher HSC abundance during aging (Pang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data from aged mice and a citation to previous work.

claim: Previous work has established a non-hematopoietic, non-endothelial, Prrx-1 mesenchymal origin of pvSSCs.
source: Previous work has established a non-hematopoietic, non-endothelial, Prrx-1 mesenchymal origin of pvSSCs (Ambrosi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: One possibility is that pvSSCs originated from osteo-plastic perivascular mural cell and pericyte populations that had ingressed into the bone marrow space during endochondral ossification in limb formation.
source: One possibility is that pvSSCs originated from osteo-plastic perivascular mural cell and pericyte populations that had ingressed into the bone marrow space during endochondral ossification in limb formation (Pearson et al., 1986; Crisan et al., 2008; James et al., 2010; Corselli et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Specific stimuli such as high levels of Bmp2 or Wnt might be able to convert pvSSCs into ocSSC-like cells.
source: Yet, specific stimuli such as high levels of Bmp2 or Wnt might be able to convert pvSSCs into ocSSC-like cells (Chan et al., 2015; Matsushita et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Available mouse strains, for example the LepR-Cre reporter line, are not able to answer open questions about SSC origins because loxP-site excision-directed fluorescence reporters permanently stay on, not necessarily reflecting the current expression of the gene driving Cre-recombinase.
source: Available mouse strains, for example the LepR-Cre reporter line, are not able to answer these open questions as we observed that the expression of tracer genes did not functionally separate SSC types. One obvious reason is that loxP-site excision-directed fluorescence reporters permanently stay on, not necessarily reflecting the current expression of the gene driving Cre-recombinase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and knowledge of reporter mouse limitations.

claim: Marker expression is dependent on the developmental stage of a given cell and is not restricted to the stem cell state as it also labels derivative downstream cell populations.
source: Marker expression is dependent on the developmental stage of a given cell and is not restricted to the stem cell state as it also labels derivative downstream cell populations.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of cell marker expression patterns.

claim: Targeting SSCs by prospectively isolating them with a combination of surface markers gives a more faithful snapshot of a given cell population, however, at the expense of not being able to fate map rare cells in situ or directly test key molecular functions.
source: In contrast, targeting SSCs by prospectively isolating them with a combination of surface markers gives a more faithful snapshot of a given cell population, however, at the expense of not being able to fate map rare cells in situ or directly test key molecular functions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the advantages and limitations of different methodological approaches.

claim: scRNAseq analysis indicated a remaining degree of cellular heterogeneity within ocSSCs and pvSSCs that will have to be further functionally resolved in future studies.
source: While our approach provides a significant advance toward highly homogeneous SSC populations, scRNAseq analysis also indicated a remaining degree of cellular heterogeneity that will have to be further functionally resolved in future studies (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Leiden clustering analysis showing subclusters.

claim: These findings may be readily translatable to the human setting through existing reports of SSC populations that have comparable characteristics.
source: Excitingly, these findings may be readily translatable to the human setting through existing reports of SSC populations that have comparable characteristics (Sacchetti et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous work on human SSCs.
